headings.text: 1. Spend Time On A Free License First
headings.body: The most important hardening step is discipline rather than configuration. A free license detects and alerts and never contains, on as many nodes as you want to install it on, so the validation period is not a trial mode you have to remember to leave: it is simply the tier. Run it across the fleet, read what it reports, and decide from evidence whether the detections are ones you would have wanted acted on. The response ceiling is a property of the license rather than a chart value, so nothing in your cluster has to change when you decide to raise it. See Operating Modes for the ladder.

The sensor requests 250m CPU and 256Mi per node and is limited to 2 cores and 1Gi . That is one pod per node rather than one per workload, so the figure to plan against is per node and does not grow with your deployment count. Measured warm and enforcing on the shipping build, across two runs: a 130.4 mCPU p95 with a 106.9 MiB working set over a 24-hour warm window, and 127.3 mCPU with 110.6 MiB over a 34-hour run. Both held a flat working-set slope, with no CFS throttling and no OOMKills. The request is sized for the 70-pod cap rather than for the engine counts these runs carried. helm upgrade pando-node-sensor ... \ --set resources.requests.cpu=250m \ --set resources.requests.memory=256Mi Check actual usage with kubectl top pod -n pando-system after a week. Raise the request before shortening the sampling cadence, never after: at the 250 ms floor the same build costs roughly four times as much CPU as at the 1000 ms default, and CPU is shared by request under contention.

headings.text: 3. Decide What Is Out Of Scope
headings.body: Eleven namespaces are excluded by default, covering kube-system and the GKE managed namespaces. Add your own infrastructure namespaces to that list: cert-manager, service meshes, CI runners, and anything else whose behaviour you do not want profiled. helm upgrade pando-node-sensor ... \ --set 'excludedNamespaces={kube-system,kube-public,kube-node-lease,cert-manager,istio-system}' Two sharp edges here excludedNamespaces: [] does not mean "exclude nothing". An empty list is read as unconfigured and falls back to the built-in eleven. If you override the list, write out the full set you want, including the defaults you intend to keep. Never list pando-system in includedNamespaces . That opt-in is read before the exclusion rules and overrides the own-component exclusion as well as the namespace list, so it puts PandoCore's own pods back under monitoring. An early soak run in that configuration took 67 false positives in six minutes, 34 of them from the controller pod. Four classes stay excluded whatever the configuration says, and includedNamespaces does not override them: the sensor's own pod, hostPID pods, hostNetwork pods, and any pod carrying pandocore.io/protect: "false" . An operator opting a namespace in has not acquired the pod owner's decision.

Both charts resolve their image tag from the chart version, so pinning the chart pins what runs. Installing an OCI chart without --version fails outright rather than drifting to the newest release, which is the behaviour you want here; keep the version explicit in whatever applies your releases. helm upgrade pando-node-sensor \ oci://us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/pandocore-prod/charts/pando-node-sensor \ --version 2.0.0 \ --reuse-values

headings.text: 5. Run The Controller With Two Replicas
headings.body: The sensor is a DaemonSet and needs no replica planning: one pod per node is the topology. The controller is the component with an availability question, because a single replica means a node drain or a rolling update is a window in which sensors have nowhere to deliver evidence. The chart defaults to two. Below two the PodDisruptionBudget does not render at all, so if you have overridden it down, restore it. helm upgrade pando-controller ... --set replicas=2

The license Secret ( pando-license in pando-system ) is the one thing worth keeping a copy of. You can always reissue from the portal, but a copy makes recovery a one-liner. kubectl get secret pando-license -n pando-system -o yaml > pando-license-backup.yaml Sensor state does not need backup Each sensor keeps working state under /var/lib/pando on its node, as a hostPath rather than a PersistentVolumeClaim, deliberately: a restored state directory is refused as older than the pod reading it. Profiles rebuild on start, which is the intent, since a profile should describe the workload running now rather than a stale snapshot. Evidence durability is the controller's job, not the node's.

Detections without a consumer are log entries. The controller owns every outbound destination, so SIEM, Slack and webhook delivery are configured once there rather than per workload, and no workload pod ever holds a third-party credential. See Controller and Evidence Format . Test the path before you need it, and confirm an alert lands where you expect.

The chart ships PrometheusRules for the conditions a sensor cannot report on its own behalf. The one to wire first is coverage: pando_node_sensor_pods_unmonitored{reason="cap"} is a gauge of pods that got no engine because the node hit its cap, and those are pods you wanted watched. It is not a capacity hint. The rules also cover the series going absent, a refusal at startup, and a cadence that has stretched past its configured interval. Absence matters most, because it is the one condition no self-report can distinguish from healthy, which is why it is alerted on from outside. On GKE managed Prometheus these rules do nothing Managed Prometheus does not honour the chart's scrape annotations, so metrics.podMonitoring.enabled=true is what makes it scrape at all. It also reads neither the alert-rules ConfigMap nor a PrometheusRule , so the rules ship and sit inert until they are converted to its own Rules resource. Port the coverage and absence rules across by hand if you run it. Those two are what tell you a node has stopped being watched, and this is the configuration in which you would least want to assume the chart had covered you. Select on the component label The sensor's own pod carries pandocore.io/protect: "false" . A Prometheus job written against protect=true matches nothing and reports a clean scrape of nothing, which is indistinguishable from healthy on a dashboard. Select on app.kubernetes.io/name=pando-node-sensor .

headings.text: 9. Use CRD Policy For Anything Non-Trivial
headings.body: Configuring a handful of deployments by annotation is fine. Managing dozens of services across namespaces with kubectl annotate is not. Commit a PandoCorePolicy resource to your GitOps repo so mode, sensitivity and alert destinations are version-controlled alongside everything else. See CRD Policy . Per-namespace integrations declared in a policy reach the controller through the destinations mirror, which the sensor chart installs by default. Setting mirror.enabled=false leaves them inert.

headings.text: 10. Understand What The Sensor Runs As
headings.body: This is the section to read before you install, and it is a real increase in node surface compared with the deprecated sidecar. The sensor runs as a hostPID DaemonSet, as uid 0, with CAP_SYS_PTRACE , mounting the node's /proc read-only and a host path for its own state. The node's PID namespace is the whole point of the topology: the sensor sits outside every pod it watches, so that namespace is the only way it sees their processes. Not compatible with restricted Pod Security, GKE Autopilot or EKS Fargate The deprecated sidecar ran unprivileged and satisfied the restricted Pod Security Standard. The sensor does not, and there is no install path on GKE Autopilot or EKS Fargate, both of which forbid hostPID . If you need those, the node sensor is not deployable for you today. Standard GKE is the configuration this release was validated on. On uid 0 specifically: it is load-bearing rather than inherited. CAP_SYS_PTRACE becomes effective through the uid-0 path, and the alternative posture is a file capability raised in-process with allowPrivilegeEscalation: true , which is more escalation surface than root with escalation switched off. Of the two postures that work, this is the narrower one. What bounds it instead is the grant. The sensor's ClusterRole holds pods get/list/watch, events create, networkpolicies create/delete/get, the three workload-owner kinds get, policies list, services list, and namespaces get scoped to kube-system . pods: patch , pods: delete and endpoints: get are withheld by name, each with its reason recorded in the chart. The cluster-wide secrets get that per-namespace integrations need does not sit on this pod at all: the destinations mirror is a separate unprivileged Deployment precisely so that grant is not held by a hostPID pod running as uid 0 on every node.

headings.text: 11. Three Annotations The Sensor Cannot Honour
headings.body: If you are migrating from the webhook, these three do nothing now: pandocore.io/full-proc-signals pandocore.io/provenance-enforce pandocore.io/node-enforcer All three were applied at admission, by rewriting a pod before it was created: the first two mutated its securityContext and the third added a hostPath volume and mount. A sensor is outside the pod and runs after it already exists, so there is no point at which it could apply any of them. The sensor warns once per pod carrying one, and the pod is still monitored. The signal coverage the first two used to buy is not lost, because the sensor already holds CAP_SYS_PTRACE on the node. They were a per-pod posture choice under a topology where each pod carried its own observer; there is no longer a per-pod posture to choose. On SELinux and Bottlerocket seLinuxLevel is empty by default and is ignored where SELinux is not the enforcing module for containers, which covers GKE's Container-Optimized OS (AppArmor) and EKS AL2023 (SELinux permissive). On Bottlerocket it is required for the file-age routes to work at all: every container runs as container_t with its own category pair, so without a clearance the sensor's pair does not dominate the target's and the path walk is refused.

Ran on a free license across the fleet long enough to judge the detections before raising the response ceiling Per-node request sized to observed usage, and raised before any cadence change rather than after Infrastructure namespaces added to excludedNamespaces , written out in full rather than emptied pando-system absent from includedNamespaces Chart version pinned explicitly with --version Controller running with replicas >= 2 , keeping its PodDisruptionBudget in effect pando-license Secret included in your Kubernetes backup process Evidence destinations configured on the controller and tested end to end pando_node_sensor_pods_unmonitored and the shipped absence rule wired into monitoring, selecting on the component label Configuration managed as PandoCorePolicy in GitOps rather than ad-hoc annotations The sensor's privilege posture reviewed and accepted by whoever owns node security Emergency procedures documented and tested (see Emergency Procedures ) Previous Operating Modes Next Upgrading

headings.text: A Workload Is Not Being Watched
headings.body: Symptom: a pod is running, but it never appears in detections and no engine was started for it. # Is there a sensor on that pod's node at all? kubectl get pods -n pando-system -o wide \ -l app.kubernetes.io/name=pando-node-sensor | grep <node> # How many engines is that node's sensor running, and is it shedding? kubectl exec -n pando-system <sensor-pod> -- wget -qO- http://localhost:9090/status # Is the pod opted out? kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'

The node is over the engine cap. Each sensor runs at most maxEngines monitored pods (70 by default). Pods beyond it get no engine, and they are shed in a stable order, so the same pods stay unwatched across restarts rather than rotating. Check pando_node_sensor_pods_unmonitored{reason="cap"} . This is the most likely cause on a dense node, and it is a coverage gap rather than a capacity hint. The pod opted out. pandocore.io/protect: "false" excludes a pod, and nothing an operator sets overrides it. Note the comparison is byte-for-byte: "False" or "0" do not opt out, so an intended opt-out may also be silently inactive. The namespace is excluded. Eleven are by default, covering kube-system and the GKE managed namespaces. Add the namespace to includedNamespaces to protect it anyway; emptying excludedNamespaces does not work, because an empty list is read as unconfigured and falls back to the built-in eleven. The pod uses hostPID or hostNetwork . Both are excluded and neither is overridable. A pod whose process view or socket table is the node's cannot have a pod-scoped baseline, so watching it on request would answer the question wrongly rather than narrowly. No sensor is scheduled on that node. The DaemonSet tolerates everything by default, so this usually means a nodeSelector was set, or the node cannot allocate the sensor's CPU request. The install preflight refuses the latter case at install time; if it was bypassed with preflight.nodeCapacity=false , the sensor pod will sit Pending instead.

headings.text: A Sensor Is Refusing Or Crash-Looping
headings.body: Symptom: the sensor pod is running but /readyz returns 503 indefinitely, or the pod is in CrashLoopBackOff . # Current and previous logs kubectl logs -n pando-system <sensor-pod> kubectl logs -n pando-system <sensor-pod> --previous # Events and exit codes kubectl describe pod -n pando-system <sensor-pod> A refusal is not a crash, and /healthz will still say 200 When the sensor refuses to monitor it parks rather than exiting, and /healthz deliberately keeps returning 200 so the kubelet does not crash-loop the refusal logs away before you can read them. /readyz is the endpoint that reports it. A pod that looks healthy in kubectl get pods can be refusing, so check readiness rather than phase. A refusal names one of eight reasons, which is also the label on the refusal metric: config , licence , siem , node_name , state_dir , cluster_limit , revoked or channel . A refusal is a configuration error and will not clear on its own. licence : the license failed validation. A signature mismatch usually means the image and the license are from different environments. An expired license needs renewal from the portal. Note the key is not trimmed, so a Secret created from a file with a trailing newline fails validation; create it with --from-literal . config : a value was rejected at startup rather than silently clamped. The most common is sampleIntervalMs below its 250 ms floor, which is refused by name. There is no 100 ms option. channel : the sensor could not establish its evidence channel to the controller. Check the controller is installed and running, and that its Service publishes the evidence port the sensor expects. The sensor composes that URL from the controller's parts rather than taking a hand-written one, so a mismatch is usually a namespace or service-name override. state_dir : /var/lib/pando could not be created or written on the node. node_name : the sensor could not determine which node it is on, so it cannot attribute evidence or be metered correctly. cluster_limit or revoked : a portal-side verdict about this cluster or license. Check the portal. The controller client certificate is mandatory The sensor mounts the controller's client certificate Secret with optional: false , so a missing Secret fails the pod rather than starting a sensor whose evidence has nowhere to go. If the pod will not start at all and the events mention a missing Secret, that is this.

The sensor requests 250m CPU and 256Mi per node, and is limited to 2 cores and 1Gi. If you have shortened the sampling cadence, raise the request to match: at the 250 ms floor the same build costs roughly four times as much CPU as at the 1000 ms default, and CPU is shared by request under contention. helm upgrade pando-node-sensor ... \ --set resources.requests.cpu=500m \ --set resources.limits.memory=1Gi

Symptom: detections firing on normal workload behaviour during batch jobs, traffic bursts or other legitimate variance. First, confirm the workload finished learning. A profile takes 30 minutes and at least 900 samples, whichever is later, and detections before that are not meaningful. Behavioural checks that rest on longer baselines keep warming for hours beyond it, so a workload that has been watched for forty minutes is not yet fully calibrated. kubectl exec -n pando-system <sensor-pod> -- wget -qO- http://localhost:9090/readyz

headings.text: Tuning options, in order of preference
headings.body: Loosen sensitivity in a PandoCorePolicy for that namespace. low , medium or high , where a higher preset is a tighter gate. This is the right lever because it is per-namespace and version-controlled. See CRD Policy . kubectl patch pandocorepolicy default -n production \ --type merge -p '{"spec":{"sensitivity":"low"}}' Put the workload in monitor . It keeps being watched and keeps producing evidence, and stops alerting, which is the right move while you calibrate rather than switching anything off. kubectl annotate deployment your-app pandocore.io/mode=monitor --overwrite kubectl rollout restart deployment/your-app Restart the workload to re-profile it. If its traffic pattern genuinely changed, the old profile no longer describes normal. There is no re-learn endpoint on the sensor; a workload re-profiles when its pods restart. Contact support. If the preset and a re-profile do not settle it, reach out. We would rather debug it with you. Sensitivity is not a per-workload environment variable any more PANDO_SENSITIVITY still exists, but on the node sensor it belongs to the DaemonSet, so it applies node-wide rather than to one workload. Use a PandoCorePolicy for per-namespace tuning, and thresholds within it for finer numeric control. Thresholds can only tighten what learning derived, never loosen it; use sensitivity to loosen.

Symptom: the sensor is ready, but /metrics looks empty or the portal dashboard shows no activity. # Metrics directly off the sensor kubectl exec -n pando-system <sensor-pod> -- wget -qO- http://localhost:9090/metrics # Is the controller receiving anything? kubectl logs -n pando-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=pando-controller --tail=100 Your Prometheus job matches nothing. This is the most common cause and the most misleading, because it reports a clean scrape of nothing, which looks identical to healthy. The sensor's own pod carries pandocore.io/protect: "false" , so a job selecting on protect=true finds no targets. Select on app.kubernetes.io/name=pando-node-sensor . Learning has not finished. Wait for /readyz to return 200. Evidence is reaching the controller but not leaving it. The controller owns every outbound destination, so an empty SIEM or Slack channel with healthy sensors is a controller configuration question rather than a sensor one. See Controller . Egress is blocked. Your cluster's NetworkPolicy or firewall may be blocking the controller's outbound calls. Check the controller's logs for HTTP errors. Per-namespace integrations are inert. Integrations declared in a PandoCorePolicy reach the controller through the destinations mirror. If mirror.enabled=false , nothing writes the destinations Secret and those integrations do nothing. The controller's own destinations are unaffected.

Symptom: a workload lost network egress and you need to understand why. Containment is a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, so it is visible and reversible with ordinary tooling: # The policy PandoCore wrote kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> # The detection that caused it kubectl get events -n <namespace> --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod> Read the evidence record in the portal's Events tab for the detection reason and severity. Check the workload's mode. If you expected it only to alert, confirm with kubectl get deployment your-app -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.metadata.annotations}' . Remember the annotation is read when the sensor starts watching a pod, so a recent change may not have applied to pods already running. If the behaviour subsides, the policy is removed automatically. You do not need to delete it by hand, and deleting it does not resolve the underlying detection. If it was clearly a false positive, see Too Many Alerts above. To stop PandoCore responding immediately while you investigate, see Emergency Procedures .

Collect the following before reaching out: kubectl version , and the chart versions from helm list -n pando-system kubectl logs -n pando-system <sensor-pod> (last 200 lines) kubectl exec -n pando-system <sensor-pod> -- wget -qO- http://localhost:9090/status kubectl describe pod -n pando-system <sensor-pod> The value of pando_node_sensor_pods_unmonitored if coverage is the question The relevant portal evidence record if a pod was contained Send to support or reply to your onboarding email thread. Previous Upgrading Next Emergency Procedures

If you are running the webhook and injected sidecars, this is the one upgrade that is not a version bump. The webhook and the sidecar are deprecated and receive no further release. Do not run both topologies at once The sensor excludes its own pod, hostPID pods, hostNetwork pods and anything carrying the opt-out label. It does not exclude a pod that already has a sidecar. Install the sensor while the webhook is still injecting and those pods are watched twice, by their own sidecar and by the node sensor, which means two sets of detections and two independent responses to the same behaviour. Follow the order below. Install the controller if you do not already run one. See Getting Started . Existing webhook installs usually have one. Stop the webhook injecting. Uninstall the webhook chart, or scale it to zero if you want to keep the release for rollback. Already-running pods keep their sidecars until they restart. Restart your protected workloads so their pods come back without a sidecar. kubectl rollout restart deployment/your-app , in batches, most critical last. Install the node sensor. It picks up every workload on each node without further labelling. Remove the old labels. pandocore.io/protect: "true" no longer does anything. Leaving it is harmless, but it reads as though it still means something. Your metered node count will change Under the webhook, the nodes that metered were the ones running injected pods. Under the sensor, every schedulable node runs a sensor and meters. A cluster that ran sidecars on 3 of 10 nodes metered 3; a DaemonSet on 10 schedulable nodes meters 10. Check Pricing against your node count before you migrate a large cluster. You can reuse the license Secret the webhook chart created rather than passing the key again: helm install pando-node-sensor ... \ --set license.existingSecret.name=pando-license Three annotations stop working at this point: pandocore.io/full-proc-signals , pandocore.io/provenance-enforce and pandocore.io/node-enforcer . All three were applied by rewriting a pod at admission, which a sensor cannot do from outside it. See Production Hardening for why the coverage they bought is not lost.

helm upgrade pando-node-sensor \ oci://us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/pandocore-prod/charts/pando-node-sensor \ --version 2.0.0 \ --namespace pando-system \ --reset-then-reuse-values Use --reset-then-reuse-values (Helm 3.14 or later) rather than --reuse-values . It keeps what you set, such as your license key, and takes the new chart's defaults for everything else. --reuse-values keeps the old chart's defaults too, so a setting a newer chart introduced can render empty. The DaemonSet rolls node by node, at most maxUnavailable at a time (one by default). While a node's sensor is restarting, the workloads on that node are not being watched, so a rollout is a brief per-node coverage gap rather than a cluster-wide one. Nothing in your workloads restarts. The capacity preflight runs on upgrade too If the new chart raises the CPU request and a node cannot allocate it, the upgrade fails rather than leaving that node's sensor Pending for ever. The message names the nodes. Either give them room, exclude them with a nodeSelector and accept that they go unwatched, or proceed deliberately with --set preflight.nodeCapacity=false .

The controller is a StatefulSet that keeps each replica's evidence spool on its own volume. The StatefulSet replaces one replica at a time, and each new pod tries to deliver what is on its spool before it accepts new evidence. helm upgrade pando-controller \ oci://us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/pandocore-prod/charts/pando-controller \ --version 2.0.0 \ --namespace pando-system \ --reset-then-reuse-values

headings.text: One-time step for controllers installed before 2026-09-28
headings.body: Controller charts published before 2026-09-28 wrote the chart version into the StatefulSet's volume claim template, which Kubernetes never lets change. A controller installed from one of them cannot be upgraded in place. helm upgrade stops with a message that begins: The live StatefulSet pando-system/pando-controller-pando-controller has a spool volumeClaimTemplate this chart cannot upgrade in place. and ends with the command to run. Tools that render with helm template , such as Argo CD, show the API server's message instead, spec: Forbidden: updates to statefulset spec for fields other than ... , and the fix is the same. To check whether your install needs it: kubectl get statefulset pando-controller-pando-controller -n pando-system \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeClaimTemplates[0].metadata.labels}' If the output includes app.kubernetes.io/version , delete the StatefulSet object once, keeping its pods and volumes, then run the upgrade: kubectl delete statefulset pando-controller-pando-controller -n pando-system --cascade=orphan helm upgrade pando-controller \ oci://us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/pandocore-prod/charts/pando-controller \ --version 2.0.0 \ --namespace pando-system \ --reset-then-reuse-values Never delete the spool volumes --cascade=orphan removes only the StatefulSet object. The controller pods keep running and the spool-* PersistentVolumeClaims are untouched. Those volumes hold evidence the controller has acknowledged and not yet delivered. The new StatefulSet finds them by name ( spool-pando-controller-pando-controller-0 and -1 ), mounts the same volumes, and delivers what is on them. Run the upgrade straight after the delete: until it runs, a controller pod that is evicted or deleted is not recreated. Afterwards, confirm the claims are the ones you had, bound to the same volumes: kubectl get pvc -n pando-system -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=pando-controller Existing claims keep their old app.kubernetes.io/version label, because a StatefulSet never relabels a claim it already created. A helm rollback to a release made before this change needs the same one-time step.

A sensor builds its profiles in memory and keeps working state under /var/lib/pando on its node as a hostPath rather than a PersistentVolumeClaim, deliberately: a restored state directory is refused as older than the pod reading it. So a sensor restart re-profiles the workloads on that node. Expect a 30-minute learning window per workload after a sensor restarts, and at least 900 samples, whichever is later. The sensor's /readyz returns 503 until it is armed. Your workloads are unaffected and keep serving traffic throughout. Profiles are not carried across versions. Detection logic changes between releases and reusing old state would conflict with new scoring. The rollout is already staggered by maxUnavailable , so you do not need to stagger it yourself. Lower it to slow a large fleet down further.

Sensor and controller do not need to match exactly. The webhook mutated pods at admission time, adding a detector container to pods labelled pandocore.io/protect: "true" . The node sensor instead watches the workloads already running on its node, so there is no admission step, no pod mutation, and no restart needed to start or stop watching a workload. The label still matters, with its sense reversed: a pod now opts out , with the exact string pandocore.io/protect: "false" . The old "true" value has no effect.
